On the titlmr hand, diphtheria is now more prevalent than it used to be, sad thin is attributed by one authority to " the ever-growing facilities for personal infec- tion which have followed upon the herding our children imputation into elementary schools at the very age at which they ire mist susceptible to this diseme.'"fhe other disesem which have shown 11Fi inCtoltiso during recent years are those connected with the nervous system. It is a mourn- ful but undoubted fact that more people now go mad than used to be the case. In fact, if we iney judge by the norm if the R 601811.11. GIMBRAL the deaths which are placed under the heading of insanity and paralysis are increasing at an appal- lingly rapid rate. According to Dr. FAIIO7kIAIIBOIf, deaths of this particular kind were at one time seldom heard of, yet there were :1,620 of them in 1105 an compared with 9:13 in 1876. Diseaaes of the heart. Bright's disesse,diabetes and cancer are maladies which are constantly claiming a larger number of victim. In fact, cantor has nearly doubled since 1876, while diabetes cmee have been tousiderably more than doubled since the same Jane. This in, in the opinion of the Nunn- NWT of the Sanitary Institate,an anremic age. Ile propounds the question why it should be so, but does not attempt to give any precise answer. That it is due to the stress and push of • competing ego is not, he says, • con- vincing answer, for the worst sufferers are often those who " are removed by fortune from the whirling maelstrom of life into quiet backwaters." "Who," he asks," have the neural - gins, and the hysterias, and the heart failures, and Use nervous pr. strati°. wl ich attack both seance alike P Not the strenuom workers in the hive, but the drones who, more by chance than design, and from lack of °pre unity rather than deliber- ate idleness, lost the healthy stimulus of occupa- tion, and spent their time on that moat wearieoine of human occupatious, trying to kill it." He does suggest, or rather hint, that the ampulla to which be refen may be partly dm to too much meat- eating, and to too little milk aunt °stelae' and fruit end vegetnbles or perhaps Gs over-pressur 0 at echo.' and, so far as one part of the population is eoncereed, to tight lacing. But he does not advocate any epeeist remedy. Ile perhaps thinks that the evils he speaks of are largely the outcome of the social conditions, mei that the cure iii more within the province of the social reformer than of the mediml practitioner or sanitarian.

There has rarely, if over before,been such • wide- spread manifeatation of esteem for • deceased townsman no was made last week on the occasion of the funeral of the late Dr. T. Starkey Smith. All classes and conditions of townspeople combined to display their regard for the memory of tin gentle- man vein was less than. week ago in the full exer- cised all nis facultim and active in th• discharge of his honourable and beneficent profession. This display of public isomerism, all the more remark- able from the foci that Dr Smith was not, in the tallest sense of the word, a public man. That I. to say, he was not, and had never been, a member of the Town Council nor ef any other public body the mem- bership of which bringr men into prominence. On the other hand, however, he could certainly be described ss one of the leading and roost influential citizen. of Warrington ache wac undoubtedly one of the hew known and most highly esteemed. His reputation and influenle were based upon his high and unblemished character se a man and upon his skill and conscientiousnees ae • physician. The universal regret at this cushion and unexpected loss of • man whose life and lablurs have been of great value to his native town have been worthily ex- pressed—by the Mayor snd others at the Town Council, by megistratas ow the bench, and by the ministers of the church of which He. Smith was a useful member, and by many others with whom be came in contact in the course of an active career.

The presentations which were made to Mr. Wm. Roberts last week were • thoroughly well deserved recognition of many years services given to the ranee of temperance in Warrington without fee or reward, The Temperance Federa- tion has since ire formation been the mainstay of the t•nipemnce cause in Warrington. and we are sure the other members of the Federation will not conxider it any disparagement when we my that Mr Roberts bas been the backbone of that organisation Mr. Robert, has certainly not lain upon shed of tones during the time he ha. been the chief official of the Federation. Ile has et one time or another been the object of scurrilous attacks and of rude denunciation.; which were not always free from malice. But he has diecharged the dab. of the office with the vigour and fearlessness which spring from • thorough conviction of the impor- tance of the work he ix engaged in and from a dirpoition which ie not to be intimbliited by the noisy clamours of theme who, to put it mildly, are net always entirely disin'erested.

There wee quite • variety of subjects under dis- cunsion at the WarringtonTown Council meeting but as there woe no t tiotion not nothing even approaching the naturo of • " ncene " the whole of the businena wan tranatacted in lit tle over an hour. The electric lighting question came fleet in order, if not in importance, and it may at once be said that the references to this matter will not NMno anybody to rich to the conclunion that Warrington I. to he, provided with the brilliant illuminant in the imme- diate future. It IR trot list the if 1111110 money decided to ap?ly for power to supply electricity, hut this, an the Mayor captained, Ina only • "formal matter." The Corporation was applying for thin prow normal order, IF, that sioborly nine might get it beforehand. The Mayor was quite right in saying that Warrington does not want another gas or water work. -in other word& that the town dnorn not want anet'ler of its public supplies to ',trolled by a company of private mono- pollee, as Om on and water undertaking were until they were lumina.' at • big price by the Oorporstion. At the IMISe time it mat be hotted that the Girporation will not be entintly satisfind with • " dog in the manger' policy with regard to electricity. The •ery fee' that electricity is being atihleetl so reVilly o, her tonsil:11111i, ion in proof that it is found to be of public advan..age for Industrial and other purposes.

The next •oblect of dierumion may perheps, partly explain the berkwardnere of the o:reparation in tackling the i.liviricity problem. That can be postponer', bui it it now clear that the erection of sow police buddinge can not be deferred mach longer. When no leam ao authority than the Florae I Secretary begins to inquire whet is being done with reopect to improving the arrow...tenon of the police it is felt to be time to none.r The Home Secretary bokle • dominating prein in thin mat- ter, fort! he is not satiofte4 he mtcht deprive the Carport' ion of the very subetantial grant which I. med towards the expellees of the police force. New police beddinge there will have to be. then, Uire, and these alone, *part from any idler rehentee at improw•ment under coneideretion, meant Con- idenble eapearUture in the war toter,.

Councillor Evans account of the experiments at Longford was as clear and candid as could be wished. It shown that the Sanitary Works Com- mittee has not yet met with the success in intro- ducing new method. of treating the material at Longford that Was at one time anticipated. The great work at Longford is, briefly speaking, to separate liquids from solids, which up to now ban been both a tedious and an unpleasant proCesr. The committee was, a few monthe ago, inclined to think that it bad discovered a speedier way of bringing about the desired separation. But some further inquiry "knocked the bottom out of their hopes "as Mr. Evans graphically put it. It was found that the separation took place all too rapidly ae, from analyme that were mad, by Meitoddock,it was discovered that the liquids were carrying sway with them substances or manurial value which hould be left behind in the solids. The results from the experiments at Longford appear,therefore o be mainly of • n.gative character solar. The committee hae obtained ROHM additional scientific information :which may be of advantage in the future, and has decided to adopt a new,form of evaporator.

The niggardliness of the County Cauncil In doling out it* grant. to Warrington in aid of technical in- etruction and the Manchester Sewage Scheme are now getting to be rather familier imblects of die- cusaion at the Council meetings, but they erg none the leas important on that account. Councillor Robots again showed clearly that Warrington has • very serious cause of eitruilaint against the County Council in regard to its gran., and that until thew, grants are revised upon a junier scale the local Technical Instruction Committee will be sort much hampered in ite work. The Manchester Sewage • Scheme has, as we pointed out last week. once more developed into a serious menace to Warring- ton interesta. It is just possible, of course, that the Manchester rstepayers may refuse to support the scheme no they did last year, sad in that event Warrington will he relihved f rout the cost and trouble of further opposition. In any case, how- ever, the River. Committee is preparing to deal with the emergency, and the Council is evidently of one mind upon the subject.
